title: Debt
hookLine: owing weighs on a soul; the Church prays for relief
tomorrow: how does a farmer with full barns end up called a fool?

cards: A payment app sends a friendly reminder. A statement sits unopened on the counter. Owing has a weight, even when the number is small.

Jesus tells a story about a man under a weight nobody could lift. A servant is brought before his king, owing ten thousand talents. The king orders him sold, with his wife and his children and all he has, to pay it.
The man falls to the floor and begs for patience, promising to pay it all. And the king…

teach.h: THE KING FORGIVES ALL OF IT.
teach.b: …lets him go. Not a payment plan. In the Douay-Rheims Bible, the lord, moved with pity, "let him go and forgave him the debt."

teach.h: A HUNDRED PENCE, BY THE THROAT.
teach.b: Then the same servant walks out and finds a fellow servant who owes him a hundred pence. He seizes him by the throat: "Pay what thou owest." The man begs in nearly the words the servant himself had just used.
No mercy. Into prison. When the king hears, he asks the question the whole story turns on: "Shouldst not thou then have had compassion also on thy fellow servant, even as I had compassion on thee?"
That's the Lord's Prayer told as a story. In Matthew's version: "forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." Luke's version says sins, then forgives every one that is indebted.
Sin is pictured as owing, and mercy as a debt written off, first received and then passed on.
That is why the two halves of the line come tied together. The Church means real money too.
The law of Moses ordered a remission of debts in the seventh year, and Saint John Paul the Second, preparing for a jubilee year, asked that the debts of poor nations be reduced or canceled.
And Paul leaves exactly one debt open: "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another."

how: Catholics pray the Lord's Prayer daily and at every Mass, asking forgiveness as they forgive; the Church has also called for relief of the debts of poor nations, notably ahead of a jubilee year.

games.q: your cousin quietly forgot the $40 you owed her. now your little brother owes you $5, and you're about to hound him for it. what does the story put first?
o: remember what was let go for you before you collect from him.
collect: the story is about paying back what you owe.
let it go only if he begs the way you would have.
games.why: the servant's sin wasn't asking for money; it was forgetting his own forgiven debt with his hands on his fellow servant's throat.

practice: Bring one debt to mind, money or otherwise: a bill, a loan from a friend, a favor never returned. Name it plainly, then choose the next small step and the day you'll take it.
If you pray, you can pray for someone carrying a debt heavier than yours, and for the people they owe.

wordCard.voice: Debt. What's owed, in money or in mercy, and in Matthew's prayer, what's asked to be forgiven, as it is forgiven to others.

orig.note: Greek: debts, things owed. Matthew's word in the Lord's Prayer.

carryVoice: Keep this one: forgive us our debts, the hundred pence let go the way the ten thousand talents were. See you tomorrow.
